items.title: FETTUCCINE: Fast and efficient brain-to-text decoding on mobile devices
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18561v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.

items.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18562v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.

items.title: Robust Long-Tailed Learning under Label Noise
items.summary: arXiv:2108.11569v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-tailed learning aims to enhance the generalization performance of underrepresented tail classes. However, previous methods have largely overlooked the prevalence of noisy labels in training data. In this paper, we address the challenge of noisy labels in long-tailed learning. We identify a critical issue: the commonly used small-loss noisy label detection criterion fails to perform effectively in long-tailed class distributions. This failure arises from the inherent bias of deep neural networks, which tend to misclassify tail class examples as head classes, leading to unreliable loss calculations. To mitigate this, we propose a novel small-distance criterion that leverages the robustness of learned representations, enabling more accurate identification of correctly-labeled examples across both head and tail classes. Additionally, to improve training for tail classes, we replace discrete pseudo-labels with label distributions for examples flagged as noisy, resulting in significant performance gains. Based on these contributions, we introduce the Robust Long-Tail learning framework, designed to train models that are resilient to both class imbalance and noisy labels. Extensive experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms previous methods, offering substantial performance improvements.

items.title: Mapping Seven Decades of Philosophy in Colombia: Dynamic Topic Modelling of Ideas y Valores
items.summary: arXiv:2412.04236v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data-driven approaches to philosophy have emerged as a valuable tool for studying the history of the discipline. However, most studies in this area have focused on a limited number of journals from specific regions and subfields. We expand the scope of this research by applying dynamic topic modeling techniques to explore the history of philosophy in Colombia and Latin America. Our study examines the Colombian philosophy journal Ideas y Valores, founded in 1951 and currently one of the most influential academic philosophy journals in the region. By analyzing the evolution of topics across the journal's history, we identify various trends and specific dynamics in philosophical discourse within the Colombian and Latin American context. Our findings reveal that the most prominent topics are value theory (including ethics, political philosophy, and aesthetics), epistemology, and the philosophy of science. We also trace the evolution of articles focused on interpreting a specific philosopher's work rather than proposing new positions, and we note a salient emphasis on German philosophers such as Kant, Husserl, and Hegel across various topics throughout the journal's lifetime. Given the journal's founding aspiration toward more original, non-exegetical philosophy, we investigate whether exegetical topics became comparatively less prominent over time. Our analysis suggests no significant decline in such topics. Finally, we propose ideas for extending this research to other Latin American journals and suggest improvements for natural language processing workflows in non-English languages.

items.title: Bidirectional Information Flow (BIF) - A Sample Efficient Hierarchical Gaussian Process for Bayesian Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2505.11294v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hierarchical Gaussian Process (H-GP) models divide problems into different subtasks, allowing for different components to address each part, making them well-suited for problems with inherent compositional structure. However, existing H-GP frameworks typically employ one-way information sharing - either top-down or bottom-up - which limits sample efficiency and slows convergence. We propose Bidirectional Information Flow (BIF), which establishes continuous two-way communication. BIF retains the modular structure of hierarchical models - the parent conditions its own posterior on child summaries, treating them as structured priors - while introducing top-down feedback to softly decompose environment observations from the parent into sub-responses. This mutual exchange improves sample efficiency, enables robust training, and allows modular reuse of learned subtask models. We prove analytically the regret of a GP with a learned kernel scales linearly with the mismatch to the true kernel, tightening in the hierarchical case to the sum of child-level errors. Ablation shows removing the downward pathway collapses child $R^2$ by up to 58%. Across synthetic, neurostimulation, and HPO benchmarks, BIF achieves up to $4\times$ higher parent $R^2$ and roughly 100% AUC improvement over vanilla GPBO, and outperforms or is the runner-up in 38/40 tests compared to the state-of-the-art baselines while supporting modular child transfer to novel composite tasks.

items.title: Robust Surrogate Modeling for Explainable Graph Neural Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2508.01925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in a wide range of graph-related learning tasks. However, explaining their predictions remains a challenging problem, especially due to the mismatch between the graphs used during training and those encountered during explanation. Most existing methods optimize soft edge masks on weighted graphs to highlight important substructures, but these graphs differ from the unweighted graphs on which GNNs are trained. This distributional shift leads to unreliable gradients and degraded explanation quality, especially when generating small, sparse subgraphs. To address this issue, we propose explaining a robust surrogate whose explanations provide a faithful proxy for those of the original model. Specifically, we train this surrogate model through an iterative re-weighting strategy that alternates between identifying explanation subgraphs and adapting the model to the resulting weighted graph distribution, supporting stable explanation refinement while preserving the validity of the soft-mask relaxation. We evaluate our method on multiple benchmark datasets using different GNN backbones and explanation methods. Experimental results show that our method consistently improves explanation quality and can be flexibly integrated with different architectures.

items.title: Structured Basis Function Networks: Loss-Centric Multi-Hypothesis Ensembles with Controllable Diversity
items.summary: arXiv:2509.02792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble learning and multi-hypothesis prediction are two complementary paradigms for improving predictive performance and robustness. This work introduces the Structured Basis Function Network (s-BFN), a loss-aware ensemble framework that unifies these paradigms through a supervised aggregation mechanism motivated by the loss-induced Bregman-centroid geometry of prediction space. The approach constructs a structured dataset of base predictions and trains a parametric combiner directly against the observed labels, with the centroidal formulation serving as a geometric reference rather than an exact centroid solver, while a diversity-control parameter regulates specialization among predictors. The proposed framework is evaluated across regression and classification tasks, including tabular data, image recognition, and large-scale temporally structured video classification. Empirical results show that s-BFN provides strong performance across the evaluated regimes and is competitive with the aggregation baselines considered in the study. The strongest gains are observed in higher-dimensional and temporally structured settings, where aggregation capacity and controlled diversity are jointly beneficial, while simpler tabular regimes exhibit earlier saturation. These results highlight a capacity-complexity-diversity trade-off rather than a strictly monotonic relationship between diversity, ensemble size, and accuracy.

items.title: Bayesian Transfer Operators in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
items.summary: arXiv:2509.22482v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transfer operators provide a linear description of nonlinear dynamical systems by propagating observables or probability distributions. In reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, these operators are represented through conditional mean embeddings, whose regularized estimator coincides with the posterior mean of Gaussian process regression. Building on this correspondence, we formulate Gaussian Process Dynamic Mode Decomposition, a Bayesian transfer-operator method that combines sparse variational Gaussian processes with kernel-based Koopman and Perron--Frobenius operator approximation. The resulting framework provides a principled route to uncertainty quantification, scalable sparse approximations, and data-adaptive dictionary learning for prediction and spectral analysis. Additionally, the model-selection formulation naturally gives rise to a forward--backward operator structure, which establishes a connection between Bayesian transfer-operator learning and time-lagged canonical correlation analysis.

items.title: Simultaneous Learning and Optimization via Misspecified Saddle Point Problems
items.summary: arXiv:2510.05241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a class of misspecified saddle point (SP) problems, where the optimization objective depends on an unknown parameter that must be learned concurrently from data. Unlike existing studies that assume parameters are fully known or pre-estimated, our framework integrates optimization and learning into a unified formulation, enabling a more flexible problem class. To address this setting, we propose two algorithms based on the accelerated primal-dual (APD) by Hamedani & Aybat 2021. In particular, we first analyze the naive extension of the APD method by directly substituting the evolving parameter estimates into the primal-dual updates; then, we design a new learning-aware variant of the APD method that explicitly accounts for parameter dynamics by adjusting the momentum updates. Both methods achieve a provable convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(\log K / K)$, while the learning-aware approach attains a tighter $\mathcal{O}(1)$ constant and further benefits from an adaptive step-size selection enabled by a backtracking strategy. Furthermore, we extend the framework to problems where the learning problem admits multiple optimal solutions, showing that our modified algorithm for a structured setting achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ rate. To demonstrate practical impact, we evaluate our methods on a misspecified portfolio optimization problem and show superior empirical performance compared to state-of-the-art algorithms.

items.title: Adversarial Attacks on Downstream Weather Forecasting Models: Application to Tropical Cyclone Trajectory Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2510.10140v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep learning-based weather forecasting (DLWF) models leverage past weather observations to generate future forecasts, supporting a wide range of downstream applications, including tropical cyclone (TC) prediction. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of these models to adversarial attacks, where subtle perturbations to upstream forecasts can alter downstream TC trajectory predictions. Crafting perturbed inputs to steer downstream outputs toward attacker-specified trajectories is a challenging problem for several reasons. First, conventional TC detection systems are opaque, non-differentiable black boxes, making standard gradient-based attacks infeasible. Second, the extreme rarity of TC events leads to a severe class imbalance problem, making it difficult to develop attack methods that produce realistic-looking cyclone paths aligned with target trajectories. To overcome these limitations, we propose Cyc-Attack, a novel method for perturbing the forecasts of DLWF models to generate adversarial trajectories. The proposed method uses a differentiable surrogate model to approximate the TC detector's output, enabling the application of gradient-based attacks. Cyc-Attack also employs a skewness-aware loss function with a kernel dilation strategy to address the severe class imbalance problem. Distance-based gradient weighting and regularization strategies are also introduced to constrain perturbations to eliminate unrealistic-looking TC paths. Our experiments show that Cyc-Attack achieves a higher true positive rate in matching the target trajectories, along with lower false alarm rates and stealthier perturbations than conventional attack methods. We further demonstrate that the adversarial upstream forecasts generated by Cyc-Attack can be leveraged as initial guidance to train an end-to-end model for learning adversarial input samples that would induce target trajectories.

items.title: CS-54k: A Paper-Grounded Corpus and Benchmark for AI Research QA
items.summary: arXiv:2510.20279v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support computer science research. To contribute reliably, these systems must be able to work with information distributed across research papers and across different aspects of the research process. However, large-scale resources that systematically organize such information into structured supervision for both model evaluation and post-training remain limited. To address this gap, we propose a systematic paper-to-QA construction pipeline that organizes information from AI research papers into structured QA pairs supported by source evidence. Using this pipeline, we construct CS-54k, a 54k-pair corpus derived from 14,474 openly licensed AI research papers. The corpus covers eight recurring paper components, including research domain, prior work, existing challenges, motivation, findings and assumptions, methods, experimental settings, and experimental results. We further derive two complementary subsets: CS-4k, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on paper-derived research QA, and CS-50k, a companion corpus for post-training. Extensive evaluations on CS-4k reveal substantial performance differences across existing LLMs and paper components, with experimental settings and results remaining particularly challenging. Moreover, post-training on CS-50k substantially improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on CS-4k, demonstrating the practical utility of structured, paper-derived supervision. Together, CS-4k and CS-50k provide a unified and scalable resource for benchmarking and improving LLMs on research paper question answering.

items.title: Amortized Inference of Multi-Modal Posteriors using Likelihood-Weighted Normalizing Flows
items.summary: arXiv:2512.04954v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a technique for posterior estimation using Normalizing Flows trained with likelihood-weighted importance sampling, the special case of neural importance sampling in which the proposal is the prior. This approach allows for the efficient inference of theoretical parameters in high-dimensional inverse problems without the need for posterior training samples. We implement the method on multi-modal benchmark tasks in 2D and 3D to check for the efficacy. A critical observation of our study is the impact of the base distribution on the modelled posteriors. We find that standard unimodal base distributions leave spurious probability \textit{bridges} between well-separated modes. We demonstrate that initializing the flow with a Gaussian Mixture Model that matches the number of target modes significantly improves reconstruction fidelity, as measured by some distance and divergence metrics. Finally, we apply this method to a curated problem in heavy flavour physics --- the extraction of the Wolfenstein parameters from the CP asymmetry in $B^0\to J/\psi\,K^0$; it is multimodal, non-Gaussian, and asymmetric in its mode weights --- and compare the results against a well-converged Markov Chain Monte Carlo reference and an exact reference computed by quadrature, using different metrics. Used as a proposal for importance sampling, the trained flow removes its remaining bias and gives the evidence.

items.title: Improving Matrix Exponential for Generative AI Flows: A Taylor-Based Approach Beyond Paterson--Stockmeyer
items.summary: arXiv:2512.20777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The matrix exponential is a fundamental operator in scientific computing and system simulation, with applications ranging from control theory and quantum mechanics to modern generative machine learning. While Pad\'e approximants combined with scaling and squaring have long served as the standard, recent Taylor-based methods, which utilize polynomial evaluation schemes that surpass the classical Paterson--Stockmeyer technique, offer superior accuracy and reduced computational complexity. This paper presents an optimized Taylor-based algorithm for the matrix exponential, specifically designed for the high-throughput requirements of generative AI flows. We provide a rigorous error analysis and develop a dynamic selection strategy for the Taylor order and scaling factor to minimize computational effort under a prescribed error tolerance. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that our approach provides significant acceleration and maintains high numerical stability compared to existing state-of-the-art implementations. These results establish the proposed method as a highly efficient tool for large-scale generative modeling.

items.title: Deep Multivariate Models with Parametric Conditionals
items.summary: arXiv:2602.01953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider deep multivariate models for heterogeneous collections of random variables. In the context of computer vision, such collections may e.g. consist of images, segmentations, image attributes, and latent variables. When developing such models, most existing works start from an application task and design the model components and their dependencies to meet the needs of the chosen task. This has the disadvantage of limiting the applicability of the resulting model for other downstream tasks. Here, instead, we propose to represent the joint probability distribution by means of conditional probability distributions for each group of variables conditioned on the rest. Such models can then be used for practically any possible downstream task. Their learning can be approached as training a parametrised Markov chain kernel by maximising the data likelihood of its limiting distribution. This has the additional advantage of allowing a wide range of semi-supervised learning scenarios.

items.title: Flow Matching from Viewpoint of Proximal Operators
items.summary: arXiv:2602.12683v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We discuss the dynamics of Optimal Transport Conditional Flow Matching (OT-CFM) under the manifold hypothesis, where the support of the target distribution is a low dimensional manifold. We first derive an exact proximal expression of the vector field, using an extended Brenier potential for the OT; the vector field can be expressed by a denoiser, which is presented as the proximal operator associated with the potential function. Based on this explicit proximal form of the vector field, we analyze the manifold stability for perturbations to initial points, using the Lyapunov exponents of the dynamics. By analyzing the local behavior with the tools in convex analysis, we show that the dynamics contract linearly in the perturbation of the normal directions to the manifold, while perturbations in the tangential directions are preserved; this implies the stability of the manifold structure to the perturbations. To justify the theoretical arguments on the population OT, we also establish the convergence of minibatch OT-CFM with neural network learning to population OT-CFM under regularity and stability assumptions, with rate exponents governed by the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support the predicted geometric behavior.

items.title: Resolving AdaBoost Cycling with LLMs: A Computer-Assisted Counterexample
items.summary: arXiv:2604.07055v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a computer-assisted counterexample to the open question of whether exhaustive AdaBoost always converges to a finite cycle, posed by Rudin, Schapire, and Daubechies in COLT 2012. The construction is based on a block-product of two small AdaBoost instances whose two factors share an exact period-2 orbit for their five-step branch maps, but whose linearized return maps have dominant eigenvalues with an irrational logarithmic ratio. This irrationality forces the sequence of instances that win each round of updates to have an irrational asymptotic frequency, which precludes convergence to a finite cycle. The resulting counterexample has 2,500 examples, weak-learning margin $1/5$, and a uniform initial distribution, and it holds under every maximizing tie rule. All finite computations in the proof are certified by rational arithmetic in SymPy, with SageMath verifying the main inequalities. We also document the collaborative workflow that led to the construction, in which GPT-5.4 Pro produced the key technical arguments; Claude Opus 4.6 summarized and critiqued different versions of that work, proposing new directions to pursue; and the authors orchestrated the process by selecting directions to prioritize, resolving ambiguities, refining each argument, and verifying the final solution. Later conversations with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra substantially simplified the solution. We present this as one of the first in-depth case studies of LLM-assisted mathematical research, resolving a long-standing open problem from theoretical machine learning, and detail the advantages and challenges of such research.

items.title: Retrieval of Coastal Biogeochemical Parameters From Near-Surface Hyperspectral Remote Sensing Reflectance Using Physics-Aware Meta-Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2605.05623v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hyperspectral in situ sensing has shown promise in retrieving aquatic water quality (WQ) parameters, such as total suspended solids (TSS), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), and total chlorophyll-a (TChl-a), for cost-effective management of coastal WQ. However, generalising such retrieval algorithms across water bodies remains challenging, as the relationship between remote sensing reflectance ($R_{rs}$) and WQ parameters can vary considerably from one region to another due to regional distinctions in environmental conditions and biogeochemistry that lead to different WQ ranges and bio-optical properties. In this study, we propose a two-stage physics-aware meta-learning framework for retrieving coastal WQ parameters from near-surface $R_{rs}$ observations. Unlike purely data-driven approaches trained solely on paired observations, the proposed framework incorporates physical knowledge through a two-stage learning process. In the first stage, a region-agnostic base model is pretrained using meta-learning on synthetic WQ--$R_{rs}$ samples generated by a bio-optical forward model parameterised with an in situ bio-optical spectral library. In the second stage, the pretrained model is fine-tuned using local samples to adapt to regional conditions. To evaluate the proposed approach, we collected in situ hyperspectral $R_{rs}$ and WQ measurements from five geographically distinct sites in Australian coastal waters.

items.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Domain Shift in Permission-Based Android Malware Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2605.09028v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning-based Android malware detectors often fail in real-world deployment due to domain shift, where models trained on one data source perform poorly on applications from another. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the generalizability and interpretability of permission-based detectors under cross-domain conditions. Using two complementary datasets (PerMalDroid and NATICUSdroid) and five ensemble classifiers, we first establish an intra-domain baseline, where models achieve over 92% accuracy, and then quantify a severe asymmetric performance drop. While models trained on PerMalDroid generalize well to NATICUSdroid (86% accuracy), the reverse direction sees a drastic drop to 73% accuracy. Explainable AI analysis reveals bimodal feature distributions and shows that feature importance is highly unstable, with key permissions losing or gaining influence across domains. The predictive feature sets for different domains are fundamentally mismatched, as models rely on different, dataset-specific permissions. Most importantly, an ablation study demonstrates that for most models, training on a noisy feature set leads to poor generalization, confirming that domain-specific artifacts are a greater obstacle than missing features. To mitigate this, we validate a hybrid training strategy based on the intersection of common features and successfully recover cross-domain performance, achieving 88% accuracy on PerMalDroid and maintaining 97% on NATICUSdroid. These findings highlight the importance of explainable, cross-domain-robust malware detection systems and provide a practical pathway toward improving real-world deployment of permission-based Android malware detectors.

items.title: Adaptive Calibration in Non-Stationary Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2605.11490v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Making calibrated online predictions is a central challenge in modern AI systems. Much of the existing literature focuses on fully adversarial environments where outcomes may be arbitrary, leading to conservative algorithms that can perform suboptimally in more benign settings, such as when outcomes are nearly stationary. This gap raises a natural question: can we design online prediction algorithms whose calibration error automatically adapts to the degree of non-stationarity in the environment, smoothly interpolating between i.i.d. and adversarial regimes? We answer this question in the affirmative and develop a suite of algorithms that achieve adaptive calibration guarantees under multiple calibration measures. Specifically, with $T$ being the number of rounds, $W$ being the unknown number of i.i.d. segments of the environment, and $C\in[0,T]$ being another unknown non-stationary measure defined as the minimal $\ell_1$ deviation of the mean outcomes, our algorithms attain $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min\{\sqrt{T}+(TC)^{\frac{1}{3}}, \sqrt{WT}\})$ for $\ell_1$ calibration error and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min\{(1+C)^{\frac{1}{3}}, W\})$ for both $\ell_2$ and pseudo KL calibration error. These bounds match the optimal rates in the stationary case ($C=0$ and $W=1$) and recover known guarantees in the fully adversarial regime ($C, W=\Omega(T)$). Our approach builds on and extends prior work (Hu et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025), introducing an epoch-based scheduling together with a novel non-uniform partition of the prediction space that allocates finer resolution near the underlying ground truth.

Using that set and following ``this feature should not be used for prediction'' reasoning, we identify highly relevant neurons in an intermediate layer and regularize their impact. This ensures that models learn to depend on informative features rather than being right for the wrong reasons, thereby improving robustness without requiring additional balanced held-out data or annotations.

items.title: Federated Learning by Utility-Constrained Stochastic Aggregation for Improving Rational Participation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.18020v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) algorithms implicitly assume that clients passively comply with server-side orchestration, sharing local model updates upon the server's request. However, this overlooks an important aspect of real-world cross-silo environments: clients are often rational agents who may prioritize their own interests, such as local model performance, over that of the global model. In settings with significant statistical heterogeneity, rational clients may opt out of the federation if the perceived benefits of collaboration fail to meet their local utility thresholds. Such attrition degrades global model performance and can lead to the collapse of the federated training process. To avoid such a scenario, in this work, we introduce FedUCA (Federated Learning by Utility-Constrained Stochastic Aggregation for Improving Rational Participation), a non-monetary framework that establishes a non-payment channel through which clients communicate their willingness to participate via their utilities. The server acts as an optimizer, identifying aggregation parameters that satisfy clients' individual rationality (IR) constraints to sustain the global model performance. FedUCA achieves this through a stochastic aggregation mechanism over Dirichlet-sampled mixture strategies, which induces an implicit utility surplus that helps satisfy participation constraints. Supported by theory and extensive experiments, FedUCA's focus on participation feasibility improves client retention and global model performance.

items.title: AMUSE: Anytime Muon with Stable Gradient Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.22432v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern deep learning commonly relies on AdamW with prescribed learning rate schedules, but recent works challenge both components: Schedule-Free optimization removes explicit schedules via iterate averaging, and Muon improves the update geometry by orthogonalizing momentum for matrix parameters. Despite Muon's strong empirical performance, its underlying mechanism remains partially understood. We study Muon through the river-valley loss landscape, where useful training progress occurs along a flat, low-curvature bulk subspace (the river), while high-curvature dominant directions form steep valley walls that induce oscillations. We empirically show that while Muon's orthogonalization accelerates river progress by increasing the bulk component, it also amplifies dominant-direction noise, causing oscillatory trajectories. Building on this, we propose Anytime MUon with Stable gradient Evaluation (AMUSE), which integrates Muon's rapid bulk progress with the stabilizing effect of Schedule-Free averaging. AMUSE uses a time-varying interpolation coefficient that initially evaluates gradients near the fast Muon sequence for rapid adaptation, then gradually shifts toward the stable averaged sequence to suppress valley-wall oscillations. As a result, AMUSE requires no learning rate schedules and supports anytime training. Across vision tasks and large language model pretraining, AMUSE consistently improves the performance-iteration Pareto frontier over (Schedule-Free) AdamW and Muon.

items.summary: arXiv:2606.05373v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable neural architecture selection is an open challenge in time-series forecasting under limited, noisy, and heterogeneous data, where standard heuristic architecture design and validation approaches fail to ensure accurate and reliable prediction and generalization. We propose EVIDENT (EVidence-based IDEntification of Neural archiTectures), a framework for architecture selection that integrates Bayesian training, evidence-based ranking, and task-specific validation under uncertainty. The framework explores the candidate architecture pool and identifies the lowest-capacity model that satisfies a prescribed validation criterion. We demonstrate this method using temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) for individualized blood glucose forecasting in type 1 diabetes patients. The results show that EVIDENT systematically rejects both under- and over-parameterized TCN architectures on population-level diabetes data, while identifying models that generalize reliably to unseen patients. When multiple architectures are competitive, the framework further supports plausibility-weighted ensemble predictions that enhance predictive performance. Compared with a random-search baseline, EVIDENT identified smaller architectures with more consistent forecasting performance on unseen patients. These findings establish EVIDENT as a strategy to neural architecture discovery, enabling reliable model selection for high-consequence forecasting in data-limited and heterogeneous settings.

Because many molecular properties are intrinsically linked to molecular size, accurately capturing the joint distribution of properties and the number of atoms is essential. However, current diffusion and flow-based models fix the number of atoms, which ultimately limits their ability to navigate this complex relationship. To address this, we introduce Morph, a flexible-size generative model for conditional and unconditional 3D molecular design based on geometric graphs. By dynamically adapting size, Morph can seamlessly integrate existing structural priors, like scaffolds, and significantly enhances property steering. We show that Morph matches current fixed-size state-of-the-art models while significantly increasing sampling flexibility. We demonstrate out-of-distribution generation in regimes where previous models fail, paving the way for enhanced generative modeling for molecular design.

items.summary: arXiv:2606.13880v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate estimation of health-state transition probabilities is essential for long-term care insurance modeling. Conventional actuarial multi-state models provide an interpretable framework but may be restrictive in capturing nonlinear relationships and accumulated health histories from irregular longitudinal observations. This paper proposes LANTERN, a history-dependent neural framework that integrates recurrent health representations, elapsed observation time, and adaptive demographic and socioeconomic attribute conditioning to estimate horizon-specific transition probabilities among Healthy, Mild disability, Severe disability, and Death states. Using longitudinal Health and Retirement Study data, we evaluate our model against a recurrent neural network, multinomial logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees, and an actuarial continuous-time Markov chain across one-, two-, and three-year forecast horizons. At the primary two-year horizon, LANTERN achieves competitive predictive accuracy and calibration, with improvements over selected benchmarks. Its aggregated transition-matrix estimates outperform multinomial logistic regression and are comparable to those of the strongest remaining benchmarks. These findings suggest that history-conditioned neural estimation provides a flexible and competitive approach to estimating horizon-specific health-state transition probabilities, with potential applications in actuarial long-term care modeling.

items.summary: arXiv:2606.28228v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Causal representation learning for time series has developed strong identifiability results in discrete-time latent causal models, but identifiability in continuous-time latent stochastic differential equation (SDE) models remains largely open. We address this gap using environment-induced shifts in diffusion covariance. We study additive-noise latent SDEs observed through an unknown nonlinear diffeomorphism, with shared drift but environment-specific diffusion covariance. We show that two diagonal diffusion regimes with pairwise distinct coordinate-wise variance ratios identify the latent coordinates up to permutation, coordinate-wise scaling, and a possible constant shift, without any sparsity assumption on the drift. We first prove this result for linear Ornstein-Uhlenbeck systems and then extend it to general additive-noise latent SDEs. Under mild smoothness, the instantaneous drift-Jacobian causal graph is identifiable up to the same permutation. We propose a two-stage estimator for latent disentanglement and optional graph recovery; experiments on synthetic systems confirm the predicted identifiability boundary, and an application to Hardanger Bridge monitoring data illustrates the approach on real sensor trajectories.

items.title: Fusion-Free Multimodal Classification with Heterogeneous Deep Ensembles
items.summary: arXiv:2607.05019v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In multimodal classification, late-fusion approaches classify concatenated modality-specific features extracted by unimodal neural networks. When modality imbalance is pronounced, various regularization techniques have been proposed to balance the learning process and overcome the inferior performance of late-fusion networks. In contrast, this work demonstrates that multimodal data can be effectively classified without any explicit modality fusion, using deep ensembles of unimodal networks. We systematically compare deep ensembles to late-fusion networks at equal parameter count and show that ensembles consistently outperform state-of-the-art late-fusion methods designed to address modality imbalance when trained from random initialization. This advantage also holds over intermediate-fusion techniques we evaluated and over hybrid methods that combine unimodal and multimodal classifiers. We propose and empirically validate a method for selecting the number of models per modality in an ensemble, avoiding computationally expensive exhaustive search. Under extreme modality imbalance and small ensemble sizes, the heuristic indicates that ensembles of unimodal models trained solely on the stronger modality are preferable. As the ensemble scales up, incorporating models from the weaker modality becomes beneficial. Both predictions align with our empirical findings. However, the heuristic becomes less reliable when the diversity of ensemble members is low. To systematically explore the challenges of optimizing multimodal models, we propose a synthetic multimodal framework that allows control over both the number of modalities and their predictive strength. Our findings are consistent across synthetic and real-world datasets. Finally, by fitting scaling laws to bimodal datasets, we estimate the asymptotic performance of ensembles.

items.title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2608.18982v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. items.summary: arXiv:2609.00518v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Antibody-specific language models pretrained via masked language modeling (MLM) learn representations that are critical for downstream sequence design and property prediction tasks. Yet, the corruption process itself is rarely leveraged as a source of inductive bias during pretraining. While preferentially masking complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) improves binding-related predictions, antibodies possess diverse biological priors over a variety of functions. Herein, we introduce function-aware masking, a family of pretraining algorithms that align mask placement with specific functional priors (e.g., from IMGT annotations or structure predictions) to shape the learned representation space. We show that these specialist masking strategies significantly improve performance on their respective objectives, yielding up to a 14% gain on structure-related tasks and up to a 5.9x improvement on CDR-related tasks. To further improve performance across multiple functional axes, we develop hybrid masking strategies that integrate multiple priors, balancing reconstruction over binding, structural, and biophysical objectives. Our results demonstrate that informed mask placement provides a parameter-free mechanism for imposing functional inductive biases in antibody language model training.

items.summary: arXiv:2609.07729v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Normative age models are trained to predict chronological age in a nominally healthy cohort. In patients, the gap between predicted and chronological age is read as disease risk. We attribute the disease-related effect size of the age gap directly to individual training samples, rather than using a prediction-level loss as the attribution target. For the Cohen's d effect size, the resulting closed-form influence functional, validated against leave-one-out retraining, ranks training samples by their effect on held-out case-control separation. Across four diseases and two biomarker modalities in UK Biobank, removing the 10% most influential training samples raises held-out disease-related effect size in every seed. It more than doubles the metabolomic-age effect for type 2 diabetes and raises the brain-age effect for multiple sclerosis by roughly a third. Random removal leaves effect size flat even at 50% removal, confirming the gain comes from which samples are removed, not how many. Flagged subjects, missed by diagnosis-based exclusion, show elevated cardiometabolic markers the model never sees, consistent with subclinical contamination of the reference cohort. For type 2 diabetes, where the method gains most, the marker recovered is HbA1c, the standard measure of blood sugar control. We release our influence-function package pyinfluence.

items.summary: arXiv:2609.18078v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Grokking, or delayed generalization after memorization, incurs substantial training steps across algebraic tasks. Cross-operator transfer from a grokked donor accelerates target acquisition, yet post-grokking AdamW continuation triggers test-accuracy relapse as unannealed updates drift across residual interfaces and decaying second moments amplify late gradients. Across depths one to three on modular arithmetic ($\mathbb{Z}_{113}$), non-Abelian $S_5$ conjugation, and real-sensory MNIST modular arithmetic, we separate representational transfer from preconditioner-governed consolidation across thirteen experimental batteries. First, co-transferring internal blocks accelerates one-layer and two-layer modular takeoff beyond boundary interfaces, while graded prefix pinning bounds depth-three drift under unannealed continuation. Second, an iso-parameter $S_5$ scaling grid separates attention head dimension from MLP width: widening two-head attention to dimension $64$ reaches $98.54\%$ cold accuracy at $427\mathrm{k}$ parameters and $85.95\%$ boundary-only transfer, while final-slot representations refine conjugation directly across blocks without an intermediate binary-product bottleneck. Third, Plateau-Gated Leaky Consolidation pairs validation-envelope step damping with leaky second-moment decay, reaching $84.85\%$ zero-leakage validation-gated risk-constrained accuracy across five pre-saturation two-layer $S_5$ suites while cutting step budget relative to hard anchoring. Fourth, transferring a grokked visual trunk and blocks to image-disjoint MNIST targets reaches $92.27\%$ and $90.76\%$ accuracy, prunes odd centroid harmonics, and reaches $90.42\%$ risk-constrained accuracy across $60/60$ branches without hyperparameter retuning.

items.title: ReCo: When to Relocate Sensor Kits under Deployment Constraints -- A NILM Case Study
items.summary: arXiv:2609.35075v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many sensing tasks obtain training labels only by deploying instruments in the field. With a limited number of sensor kits, a collection deadline, and measurement downtime at every move, the collector must repeatedly decide whether to stay at the current site or relocate. We study this decision in non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM), which estimates the power drawn by individual appliances from a home's main meter and is trained on data from homes temporarily fitted with appliance-level sub-meters. In NILM, appliance usage varies with the appliance, season and climate, and the value of new data depends on how diverse the combinations of target operation and background load are. To address this, we propose a constraint-based relocation framework and instantiate it for NILM as ReCo (Relocation by Coverage gain). ReCo counts new operating regimes in a joint target--background feature space, forecasts each home's future gain from the data collected so far, and each night weighs the gain of staying against the gain of moving elsewhere after the downtime. In replayed deployments on the Plegma dataset under two kit counts and two downtime costs, ReCo outperforms fixed-dwell and count-based schedules and a threshold rule using the same metric in every setting. Its advantage is not explained by collecting more days alone and is consistent with allocating the days to more valuable homes and periods.

items.title: When a Flatness Proxy Is Not a Function: Robustness Certificates and Training Interventions
items.summary: arXiv:2609.38540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A valid curvature upper bound need not justify either a robustness certificate or an intervention on an intrinsic predictor property. We demonstrate this distinction for a last-layer relative-flatness proxy used in both settings. First, empirical-risk stationarity does not eliminate pointwise first-order loss terms: at a finite global empirical-risk minimum, the retained certificate expression underestimates a loss increase by over $210\times$. We derive a globally valid, gauge-invariant feature-space repair. Second, common-row softmax shifts preserve predictions and the exact contraction while making the proxy unbounded. Even standard reference-class choices double it on average relative to the centered representation. For a single fixed-feature example with at least three classes, scalar retuning generically cannot align the induced probability updates. Row centering gives the orbit-minimized bound and restores value and full-model gradient invariance under this symmetry. Across 45 paired one-step tests on algorithmic and image models, amplified shifts separate raw-regularized predictors while quotient-regularized predictors remain aligned. Long-horizon CIFAR-10 experiments show substantial, reversible suppression of generalization, while evidence for selective delay after memorization is less consistent. Together, these results show that validity as a curvature upper bound does not by itself justify either inversion into a robustness certificate or differentiation into an intrinsic training intervention.

items.title: Lightweight Semantic EEG Foundation Model for Frozen Cross-Disorder Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.05503v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large-scale EEG foundation models have demonstrated promising transferability across neurological disorders, but often require millions of parameters and substantial computational resources. In this paper, we present the Universal Semantic EEG Foundation Model (USE-FM), a lightweight EEG foundation model that learns transferable neural representations through self-supervised signal reconstruction on the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus (TUEG). After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and evaluated on two clinically distinct downstream tasks, abnormal EEG detection (TUAB) and epileptic seizure recognition (TUEP), using a unified frozen-transfer protocol against recent EEG foundation models, including LUNA-Base and CBraMod. With only 1.46 million parameters, approximately one-fifth the size of existing models, USE-FM achieves competitive overall performance, including strong sensitivity and F1-score on TUEP (SEN $75.00 \pm 14.14$, F1 $70.37 \pm 4.01$), while maintaining competitive performance on TUAB (AUC $85.24 \pm 5.61$). Beyond downstream classification, latent representation analysis using $k$-means clustering together with PCA and t-SNE demonstrates that USE-FM learns organized semantic EEG representations comparable to substantially larger foundation models. These results suggest that large-scale self-supervised pretraining enables lightweight architectures to learn transferable semantic EEG representations, providing a computationally efficient foundation for cross-disorder analysis and future clinical decision support in neurological disorders.

items.title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10850v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As AI models move toward clinical decision-making and personalized treatment, understanding \emph{what} a model learns is important beyond predictive accuracy alone. We investigate whether personalized latent dynamics reveal clinically associated differences even when predictive fit is similar. A lightweight CNN--Transformer EEG foundation model pretrained on the Temple University EEG Corpus (TUEG) extracts segment-level representations. Using the Temple University Epilepsy Corpus (TUEP), representations are mapped to a shared latent-state space, and sparse multinomial logistic transition distributions (mLTD) are fit independently to each subject to obtain personalized transition-dependency graphs $W_n$. Analyses include $n{=}198$ subjects (99 epilepsy / 99 non-epilepsy). At $k{=}4$, epilepsy subjects exhibit substantially denser learned dependency structure ($p{=}1.1\times10^{-7}$), with the same pattern at $k{=}6$ (19.90 vs. 13.46; $p{=}5.2\times10^{-5}$). Graph-derived features provide moderate group discrimination under 5-fold subject-wise cross-validation (AUROC 0.68 at $k{=}4$; 0.65 at $k{=}6$). In contrast, held-out log-likelihood is nearly identical between groups at $k{=}4$ ($-0.992$ vs. $-0.991$; $p{=}0.95$), with similarly matched next-state prediction (AUROC 0.855 vs. 0.861; $p{=}0.54$). Thus, similar predictive fit does not imply similar learned dynamics: groups can be comparably predictable while differing substantially in the internal dynamical structure learned by personalized models. This distinction motivates evaluating learned structure alongside predictive performance in personalized clinical models.

items.title: PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Testing Graph Neural Networks on Unseen Patterns
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15020v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: PATTERN asks graph neural networks to find a planted subgraph in a new host graph. The hosts change, but the benchmark draws just 100 patterns and reuses them across training and test splits. A lookup that extracts these patterns from the training labels achieves 96.6% class-weighted accuracy on the official test split, above every published result, without fitting a model or consulting the generator. On unseen patterns, the same lookup scores 50.6%. A matcher that also uses the generator reaches 99.2% on the official split. Among five graph networks we retrained, GRASS and PPGT go from the top two on the official split to the bottom two on unseen patterns. Each loses 8.1 percentage points even when familiar and unseen patterns are matched in size. Logistic regression on two-hop node statistics scores above every run of the five networks on unseen patterns. For CKGConv, the advantage follows the training patterns: it reappears with each of three independently drawn pattern libraries and disappears when every training and validation graph gets a new pattern. Generator-based inference also scores 82.3% on CLUSTER, compared with a published best of 81.6%. On Minesweeper's released board, four of eight planned chains produced samples within the time budget; none converged, but their pooled predictions reached 99.86% ROC AUC, above the published best of 99.55%. PATTERN's official split tests its intended task of finding familiar patterns in new graphs. We recommend reporting the same checkpoint's score on unseen patterns alongside it.

items.title: Mode Dynamics: A Framework for Neural Network Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Mode Dynamics, a framework that connects coordinated parameter motion during neural network learning to changes in model outputs. Starting from a recorded parameter trajectory, we decompose its updates into collective modes and map each mode to its state-dependent output effect. The framework organizes this link through three mechanisms. Decomposition identifies collective modes in parameter motion and their time-varying amplitudes. Reconstruction tests whether the effects induced by those modes recover local and accumulated output change. Concentration quantifies how behavioral contribution is distributed across modes. Controlled scalar regression and next-token experiments directly test these mechanisms. They show that small sets of leading modes reconstruct behavior, induced effects depend on the training path, and modal complexity varies with task and data. In a controlled induction task, suppressing the leading modes during training impairs held-out accuracy, whereas matched controls do not. We then evaluate the framework on held-out image and language-model outputs using CIFAR-100 autoencoding and a public Pythia-70M pretraining trajectory. Across these settings, the results connect compact modal subspaces of recorded parameter motion to evolving behavior.

items.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40304v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, indicating that the gain concentrates in the time period adjacent to the estimation window. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.

items.title: Watch Your Step: Adam's Margin Maximization Bias Depends on the Learning Rate Schedule
items.summary: arXiv:2611.01929v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the implicit bias of Adam and its similarity to sign gradient descent on homogeneous models in binary classification tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we uncover that these depend on the learning rate schedule. While previous works studied strongly decaying learning rate schedules $\eta(t)=\mathrm o \left(t^{1/L-1}\right)$, where $L$ is the homogeneity degree, and showed $\ell_\infty$-margin-maximization biases, we focus on the more common complementary regime, including constant and weakly decaying schedules. For a polynomial schedule $t^{\alpha}$ and homogeneity degree $L$, we show that when $\alpha > \frac 1L - \frac12$, Adam has no trajectory-independent margin-maximization bias for deep linear networks (in the KKT sense): first, there is no non-trivial, locally Lipschitz, convex implicit regularizer in this setting, including any squared norm. Second, on width-$1$ networks, the result holds without requiring convexity, implying that any implicit regularizer for wide networks must be trivial when restricted to a width-$1$ network. Nevertheless, we positively characterize the implicit bias in this regime as maximizing a trajectory-dependent weighted-$\ell_2$ margin for any $L$-homogeneous model. The fundamental mechanism behind our results is convergence of Adam's preconditioner to a trajectory-dependent vector, which also allows showing that the limiting parameter direction depends on initialization. In the intermediate regime $\frac 1L - 1 \leq \alpha \leq \frac1L - \frac12$ we prove an $\ell_\infty$ bias, conditional on gradient directional convergence to a full-support vector. Of independent interest, we establish a loss decay rate for full batch Adam on general homogeneous models, whose leading order depends only on the second-moment parameter.

items.title: FedSharp: Byzantine Robust Decentralized Federated Learning Under Noisy Channel
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05546v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) eliminates the central aggregation server but remains vulnerable to non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise. We show that channel noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes and becomes increasingly significant as the learning rate decays. Moreover, accumulated noise enables Byzantine attackers to exploit loss-based model selection by mimicking the average of the honest models. To address these challenges, we propose FedSharp (screened, hop-aware, averaged, ranked, proximal), a robust DFL framework. In FedSharp, each node keeps the latest models received from its 2b predecessors, which guarantees at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. FedSharp screens suspicious models using their deviations from the coordinate-wise median, averages the b lowest-loss candidates to reduce the fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b, and applies hop-aware gradient-norm regularization and proximal training to mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift. Experiments on a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes show that FedSharp achieves 93.5 to 94.9 percent accuracy on MNIST, compared with 29.4 to 38.1 percent for a state-of-the-art single-model-selection benchmark, and 32.8 to 48.8 percent on CIFAR-10, compared with 10.0 to 30.5 percent, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST, FedSharp comes within 1.3 percentage points of the benchmark operating without channel noise, and exceeds it under the hidden attack.

items.title: Who Pays for the Knowledge Models Copy? Model Collapse as Lossy Transmission and Rogers' Paradox
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06022v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative models trained on the output of earlier models lose knowledge across generations, rare knowledge first. The remedies that work all bring in information from outside the loop, such as fresh human data, verifiers, or curators, and the theory of model collapse treats that supply as given. We argue that cultural evolution has a theory of the supply, and that it distinguishes two ways copying loses knowledge. In a fixed world, copies are lossy, as in Henrich's account of skill loss in small populations. In a changing world, even perfect copies go stale, which is Rogers' paradox. We write both as one chain with separately measurable parameters and test it on lineages of language models (word trigrams and a character transformer on two books, and OPT-125m on wikitext-2, on arXiv abstracts written after its pretraining, and on a world of 2,000 fictional facts that change at a set rate). In a fixed world, neutral drift on word frequencies predicts, with no free parameter, the rare-word coverage of every trigram lineage to within 0.03. In the fact world, the model's accuracy falls and its outdated answers rise with the rate of change; the chain calibrated on the static world predicts both for mid- and low-frequency facts to within 0.03 on average, with the rate of change set, not fitted. Models that inherit their weights keep more in a static world and carry more outdated facts in a changing one, as Rogers' theory says of individual memory. Finally we close the loop with the people who write the data. When they can ask the model instead of finding out, the model ends up exactly as reliable as finding out is costly, and in both regimes someone must keep paying to learn; we give the share in closed form, extend it to lossy copying, heterogeneous costs, aggregating models, and users who check, and show when checking is a stable way out.

items.title: PINR-ESI: Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Implicit Neural Representation Framework for EEG Extended-Source Imaging
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06700v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: EEG extended-source imaging aims to localize active cortical regions and characterize their extent, yet supervised inverse networks typically depend on synthetic EEG-source pairs and may be sensitive to synthetic-to-real mismatch. We propose a physics-informed self-supervised implicit neural representation (INR) framework for spatial source reconstruction without paired source labels or simulation-based supervised pretraining. The lead-field matrix encodes the source-to-sensor volume-conduction model and constrains the INR through agreement between predicted and measured EEG. Cortical current density is represented as a continuous coordinate-based neural field. Forward EEG prediction samples the field at cortical vertices and applies local smoothing before lead-field mapping. A classical inverse estimate provides warm initialization and observation-specific spatial guidance through prior-guided support regularization. Simulations across varying SNRs, source extents, and source counts showed low spatial dispersion and good localization performance. Quantitative evaluation on clinical EEG recordings from epilepsy patients and qualitative analysis of scalp EEG during intracranial stimulation supported feasibility for real-world source imaging. These findings suggest the potential of physics-informed self-supervised INR for extended-source imaging.

items.title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
items.summary: arXiv:2611.10307v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length. We recommend length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, style-matched post-cutoff controls, and cross-family calibration.

items.title: Profile-Based Auditing of Domestic Violence Survey Selection Across South Asia
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15106v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Domestic violence (DV) data in the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) are collected through a specialized module whose household-level sampling and privacy requirements create a distinct observation process. We ask whether demographic, socioeconomic, and household characteristics form reproducible population profiles and whether these profiles contain information about selection into the DV module across South Asia. Using DHS Individual Recode data for 796,374 women aged 15-49 across Afghanistan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, and Pakistan, we harmonize 61 numeric and 8 categorical features, reduce the profile space with PCA, and identify six interpretable profiles. We then evaluate 22 machine-learning models under primary-sampling-unit-aware holdout validation. The best model, HistGradientBoosting, achieves ROC-AUC 0.9167 and PR-AUC 0.9612, versus 0.8475 and 0.9203 for a design-only baseline. Adding woman-level characteristics yields the largest incremental gain, while explicit interaction terms add little out-of-sample performance. Country-specific analyses reveal substantial heterogeneity, and leave-one-country-out evaluation shows that transferability of the incremental profile signal is limited. These results demonstrate that interpretable ML can audit differential coverage in sensitive survey modules beyond the formal sampling design.

items.title: Stealthy, High-Impact False Data Injection Attacks in Smart Grid Using Physics-Constrained GAN with Limited System Knowledge
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15162v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: False data injection (FDI) attacks can distort power system state estimation while retaining plausible measurement patterns. Existing FDI methods trade stealth for impact or vice versa. They often assume access to internal grids, all-bus sensing, or defender models. In this paper, we propose a detector-agnostic physics-constrained generative adversarial network (PCGAN) that learns decoupled power-flow sensitivities from historical measurements of deployed sensors. The learned active-power-angle and reactive-power-voltage-magnitude relationships guide perturbations restricted to compromised channels, while adversarial training promotes realistic spatiotemporal patterns. We implement PCGAN and seven existing FDI attacks on the IEEE 300-bus system using one year of observed hourly demand from PJM Interconnection, a regional transmission organization in the United States, and synthetic bus-level load profiles. We compare their performance across 10%, 30%, 60%, and 100% compromised sensors. Attack stealth is assessed against ten machine-learning (ML) detectors and conventional bad-data detection (BDD) methods, while physical impact is quantified through nonlinear alternating-current weighted least-squares state estimation. PCGAN achieves 84.28% mean ML evasion and 22.31% mean spatial load misperception across the four scenarios. Its mean stealth-impact trade-off score reaches 18.69%, compared with 5.61% for the strongest competing attack. PCGAN also achieves 83.45% chi-square BDD evasion and 86.02% largest-normalized-residual BDD evasion. These results demonstrate a favorable stealth-impact balance under varying sensor-access levels and provide challenging attack cases for evaluating FDI detectors.

items.title: Detection Is Not Early Warning: Evaluating Token-Level Alarms on Language Model Failures
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many failures of language models begin at a specific token, the onset. A monitor that reads the model during generation can classify the finished response, detect the failure once it is under way, or warn before it begins, and only a warning leaves time to stop or steer the generation. Monitors are usually evaluated with response-level metrics such as AUROC, which ignore when the monitor fires. We introduce PREWARN, an evaluation protocol for any failure with an annotated onset. It calibrates each monitor's threshold on validation data to an error rate chosen for the application, runs the monitor, and scores its alarms relative to the onset on all three tasks. As a case study we apply it to repetitive degeneration in three open language models, with early warning as the main task, using linear probes on activations and six untrained baselines. Response-level metrics saturate on this failure, and a rule that reads only the response length scores almost perfectly, while probes that AUROC ranks as equal warn very differently under PREWARN. Probes warn before the onset on most degenerate responses of two of the three models, low-rank adapters below the probe more than double the share of tokens just before the onset that it flags, largely by flagging degenerate responses long before the onset, and no untrained baseline warns much more often than random alarms. We release the probes with calibrated thresholds at https://huggingface.co/collections/marcodene/prewarn-degeneration-probes

items.title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
items.summary: arXiv:2611.16934v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

items.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17108v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a 4 GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an 8 GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, llama.cpp's K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. LazyWeights keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At 1% and 3.5% perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are 5.7-31.4% smaller than the best llama.cpp format. A bit-exact 0.21 mm^2 ASIC decoder unit (1 GHz, 7 nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to 36% and 38% (54% and 44% with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, LazyWeights needs 58-64% less time and 53-57% less energy per token than CPU llama.cpp, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6x faster at 3.89 bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).

items.title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
items.summary: arXiv:2611.17143v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study data poisoning attacks on logistic regression with $\ell_2$-regularization, where an attacker chooses the features of a fixed number of injected observations with prescribed labels to maximize the logistic loss on the clean training data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem yields an exact reformulation through its first-order optimality conditions. Using convex conjugacy of the softplus function, we replace the sigmoid relations by a single convex optimality-gap inequality and express the attacker's objective as a concave function. A change of variables makes the stationarity condition affine, leaving bounded bilinear equalities as the only nonconvex constraints. We derive finite bounds on all variables involved in these equalities, including a global bound on the coefficient norm and tighter bounds obtained by preprocessing based on convex optimization. Experiments on eight binary classification datasets evaluate attack effectiveness and compare the two reformulations when solved with SCIP. Attacks obtained by local optimization degrade predictive performance on most datasets, while the convex-analytic formulation produces substantially stronger reported dual bounds within a fixed time limit.

items.title: Bias-Optimal Bounds for Stochastic Gradient Descent
items.summary: arXiv:2505.17965v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The non-asymptotic analysis of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) typically yields bounds that decompose into a bias term and a variance term. In this work, we focus on the bias component and study the extent to which SGD can match the optimal convergence behavior of deterministic gradient descent. Assuming only (strong) convexity and smoothness of the objective, we derive new bounds for the full range of constant step-sizes $\gamma L \in (0,2)$. This includes critical and large step-size regimes that were previously unexplored without additional variance assumptions, in both the convex and strongly convex cases. Those bounds are bias-optimal, in the sense that the bias term coincides with the worst-case rate of gradient descent, for all non-critical step-sizes. For critical step-sizes, we show that no bounds can be obtained with an optimal bias term, but that this optimal bias can be approximated arbitrarily closely. As an immediate application, we provide new complexity bounds for the Stochastic Proximal algorithm, without the need of regularity assumptions.
